definition: The bigger forced bet, posted by the player two seats left of the button. Bets are measured in big blinds, so "2.5bb" means 2.5 times the big blind.
example: In a $1/$2 game, 1bb = $2 and a 2.5bb open is $5.

definition: The two forced bets posted before the cards are dealt: the small blind (half a big blind) and the big blind. They create a pot to fight for.
example: Each hand starts with 1.5bb in the pot: 0.5bb from the SB and 1bb from the BB.

definition: Where you sit relative to the dealer button. It decides when you act. Acting later is an advantage because you see what others do first.
example: The button acts last on every street after the flop, which makes it the best seat.

definition: Acting after your opponent on the flop, turn and river. You get to see their action before deciding.
example: BTN calls a CO raise: the BTN is in position for the rest of the hand.

definition: Acting before your opponent after the flop. You must decide without knowing what they will do, which makes hands harder to play.
example: The blinds are out of position against everyone except each other.

definition: The first seat to act preflop, just left of the big blind. With 8 players behind, it needs the tightest range.
example: In 9-max, the seats after UTG are UTG+1, MP, LJ, HJ, CO, BTN, SB, BB.

definition: The two middle seats before the cutoff. Ranges here are wider than early position but tighter than the cutoff and button.
The seat just right of the button. Only the button and blinds act after it, so it opens a wide range.
The dealer seat. It acts last after the flop in every hand, which makes it the most profitable seat at the table.
example: The button opens almost half of all hands when folded to.

definition: The first raise in a hand when everyone before you folded. RFI stands for "raise first in".
example: UTG and UTG+1 fold, MP raises to 2.5bb: MP opened.

definition: Just calling the big blind instead of raising when nobody has raised yet. The charts in this app never limp: raising wins the pot more often and keeps the initiative.
All the hands a player could have in a spot. You don't put opponents on one exact hand, you think about their whole range.
example: "UTG's opening range" = every hand UTG would open, like 77+, ATs+, KQo…

definition: The first re-raise before the flop. The big blind counts as the first bet, the open is the second, so re-raising it is the third bet.
example: UTG raises to 2.5bb, you raise to 7.5bb: you 3-bet.

definition: A re-raise of a 3-bet. Usually a very strong hand, or a bluff with a hand that blocks strong hands (like A5s).
example: You open to 2.5bb, BTN 3-bets to 7.5bb, you make it 16.5bb: a 4-bet.

definition: Calling a raise instead of re-raising.
example: Facing a CO open, the BTN flats with 99 instead of 3-betting.

definition: An open from a late seat (CO, BTN, SB) mainly to win the blinds without a fight. Steals use wide ranges.
Calling or 3-betting from the blinds instead of folding to a raise. Because the blinds have chips in already, they get a discount and can defend many hands.
example: BTN raises to 2.5bb. In the BB, you call 1.5bb more with K7s: you defend.

definition: A 3-bet after someone opened and someone else called. The opener and caller are both squeezed in the middle.
example: CO opens, BTN calls, you 3-bet from the SB: a squeeze.

definition: Your hand shares a card with a better hand that has a stronger kicker. When you both hit, you usually lose big.
example: KJo vs AKo: whenever both hit a king, AK has the better kicker. Before the flop, KJo has only about 25% equity against AK.

definition: The side card that decides the winner when two players have the same pair.
example: A-K vs A-9 on an A-7-2 board: both have a pair of aces, the king kicker wins.

definition: A card in your hand that makes certain opponent hands less likely, because you hold one of the cards they need.
example: Holding an ace cuts the number of AA combos from 6 to 3 and AK combos from 16 to 12.

definition: Suited (s) means both cards are the same suit; offsuit (o) means different suits. Suited hands can make flushes, which adds a few percent of equity.
example: AKs = ace-king of the same suit. AKo = ace-king of different suits.

definition: Cards ten or higher: A, K, Q, J, T. Two broadway cards make strong top pairs and can make the A-K-Q-J-T straight.
Two suited cards next to each other in rank, like 98s or 65s. They make straights and flushes, which are easy to play well after the flop.
Two cards with a gap between them, like 97s (one gap) or 86s (two gaps). They make fewer straights than connectors.
Three of a kind made with a pocket pair. A pocket pair flops a set about 1 time in 8. "Set mining" means calling with a small pair hoping to hit one.
example: You hold 55 and the flop is K-5-2: you flopped a set of fives.

definition: The best possible hand on the current board. The "nut flush" is the ace-high flush.
The lowest straight: A-2-3-4-5. Small suited aces like A5s can make it.
How easy and profitable a hand is to play after the flop. Suited and connected hands have good playability; offsuit, disconnected hands have bad playability.
Your share of the pot if all the cards were dealt out with no more betting, i.e. your chance to win.
example: AA vs KK all-in preflop: AA has about 82% equity.

definition: The price of a call compared with what you can win. To call profitably, your equity must be at least: call ÷ (pot after your call).
example: BB facing a 2.5bb open: pot is 4bb, you call 1.5bb, final pot 5.5bb. You need 1.5 ÷ 5.5 ≈ 27% equity.

definition: A bet or raise made because you expect worse hands to call. The opposite of a bluff.
example: 3-betting QQ against a CO open is for value: many worse hands continue.

definition: A bet or raise with a hand that is probably behind, hoping better hands fold. Good preflop bluffs still have backup, like blockers or straight and flush potential.
Being the last player who bet or raised. The player with the initiative can often win the pot with one more bet after the flop.
A bet on the flop by the player who made the last preflop raise.
A wet board has many possible draws (straights, flushes), so hand strength changes a lot on later cards. A dry board has few draws.
example: Wet: J♥ T♥ 8♣. Dry: K♠ 7♦ 2♣.
